## Incident Report — MTA 2024-07-30 Traffic Analysis Exercise

### Victim Host

| Field | Value | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| IPv4 | 172.16.1.66 | Consistent source IP across all suspicious flows |
| MAC | 00:1e:64:ec:f3:08 | ARP (`arp.src.proto_ipv4==172.16.1.66`) and Ethernet source on all frames from 172.16.1.66 |
| Windows hostname | DESKTOP-SKBR25F | NBNS Workstation/Server service records from 172.16.1.66; also embedded in the malware beacon itself |
| Logged-in user | ccollier | Embedded in malware beacon field 5 (see below); domain is `wiresharkworkshop.online` (AD domain, confirmed via LDAP/Kerberos/CLDAP traffic to DC 172.16.1.4, hostname WIRESHARK-WS-DC) |
| OS | Microsoft Windows 11 Pro, 64-bit | Reported by the malware in its own beacon string |

### Malware Family

**STRRAT** (Java-based RAT/backdoor, commonly delivered via malspam and disguised as a "password-less" trojan; abuses a `.crimson` file extension for ransomware-style file renaming in some builds).

**Attribution confidence: signature-confirmed** — not from an external IDS signature (none was provided with this evidence set), but from the malware's own plaintext C2 check-in protocol, which literally names itself:

```
ping|STRRAT|1BE8292C|DESKTOP-SKBR25F|ccollier|Microsoft Windows 11 Pro|64-bit|Windows Defender||1.6|US:United States|Not Installed|1 Sec
```

This is TCP stream 83 (`tcp.stream==83`, `ip.addr==141.98.10.79`), a plaintext, pipe-delimited beacon sent every ~5 seconds for the full 585-second capture. Fields decode as: `ping | <family> | <bot ID> | <hostname> | <user> | <OS> | <arch> | <AV product> | <active window (base64)> | <client version> | <geo> | <"Not Installed"> | <uptime>`. Later beacons include `UHJvZ3JhbSBNYW5hZ2Vy` in the active-window field, which base64-decodes to `Program Manager` (idle desktop). The bot ID `1BE8292C` is stable across the entire session.

### Delivery Chain (partial — TLS-encrypted, no decryption keys available)

Immediately preceding the first C2 check-in (t=76.99s), the host resolved and connected to:

- `github.com` (140.82.113.3:443) at t=64.05s
- `objects.githubusercontent.com` (185.199.110.133:443) at t=64.83s — 828 KB transferred to the host
- `repo1.maven.org` (199.232.196.209:443) at t=68.01s — 8.87 MB transferred to the host (STRRAT is Java-based; this volume is consistent with fetching a JAR and/or JRE dependencies)

All three sessions are TLS 1.2/1.3 and cannot be inspected further without session keys, so no specific download URL or file hash can be grounded from this capture. First C2 beacon fires ~9 seconds after the maven.org transfer completes, which is consistent with these three domains being the delivery/staging chain, but this link is circumstantial (timing-based), not content-confirmed.

At t=77.87s, the host also queried `ip-api.com` and issued `GET http://ip-api.com/json/` to 208.95.112.1 — a plaintext HTTP geolocation lookup performed 6 seconds before the first C2 beacon and consistent with STRRAT's known environment-fingerprinting behavior (the beacon itself reports `US:United States` as a field).

### Indicators of Compromise

```json

  },

  "attribution_confidence": "signature-confirmed",
  "iocs": [
    {
      "type": "c2_endpoint",

    },

      "evidence": "DNS query + plaintext HTTP GET /json/ to 208.95.112.1 at t=77.96-78.01s, ~6s before first C2 beacon; matches STRRAT geo-fingerprinting behavior (beacon reports 'US:United States')"
    },

Roughly 9 seconds after TLS sessions to github.com, objects.githubusercontent.com, and repo1.maven.org (likely payload staging, not decryptable in this capture) and a geolocation lookup against ip-api.com, the host began a persistent plaintext beacon to 141.98.10.79:12132 that explicitly self-identifies as STRRAT with bot ID 1BE8292C, continuing every ~5 seconds for the remainder of the capture."

**Note on completeness:** no file was transferred in the clear (all suspected staging traffic is TLS-encrypted), so no SHA256 hash or delivered file name can be grounded in this capture. No IDS/Suricata alert export was present alongside the pcap in the evidence directory — attribution rests entirely on the malware's self-identifying plaintext C2 protocol.
